blocks.text: The Report That Builds Itself

You've probably worked with Excel and struggled with a report that eats your Friday afternoons. You manually click through it cell by cell, tracing where the numbers come from, and hoping nothing important hides on tab 3.

Claude for Excel changes that! Over this course, you'll get formulas explained and fixed, messy exports cleaned, pivot tables and dashboards built by describing them — until that Friday report assembles itself while you review.
Let's get started!
Meet Claude for Excel
Claude for Excel is an add-in that puts Claude in a sidebar right inside Excel. It reads the workbook you have open — every tab of it — and answers questions about it in plain language.
Scenario: The Tracker You Inherited

Imagine you're the operations coordinator at Northframe, a furniture retailer with a dozen stores. A colleague leaves the company, and their sales tracker lands on you: three tabs, zero notes, and a monthly report due next week.
The usual way through is slow — clicking cell after cell, tracing formulas by hand. Let's try a different approach with Claude for Excel!

Claude for Excel comes with a paid Claude plan. No plan right now? Keep going: every exercise in this course shows you Claude's real replies, so you can learn the moves now and install whenever you're ready.
blocks.title: Before You Install

blocks.text: Get Set Up
Setup is a one-time job: open Excel on the web platform, then open the App menu on the left, and click More apps.
Find "Claude by Anthropic for Excel" on Microsoft's add-in marketplace and add it.
Then sign in with your Claude account.
The add-in runs in Excel on the web, Windows, Mac, and iPad. In this course, you'll practice with Excel on the web.
After the guided setup process, Claude appears in a sidebar next to your sheet, ready to open the workbook.
Your First Question
The tracker is open, and the sidebar is waiting — the smartest first move is orientation: have Claude describe the workbook before you change or trust anything.
The empty sidebar greets you with a few chips, like "/audit-xls" and "/clean-data-xls". These are Skills — reusable instructions that help Claude repeat a task consistently each time.
Click one, and a full prompt appears in the reply box, with a placeholder left for you to fill.
For a workbook you've never seen, "/audit-xls" is the right chip: it sweeps every formula, reference, and format for problems.
Since you barely know this file, you'll add one line of your own before sending. Let's practice!

Formulas You Can Finally Trust
Last lesson, you learned to ask a workbook what it does, and to check every answer against its own cells.
This lesson dives deeper into formulas. By the end, you'll read, fix, create, and test them — without writing a single one by hand.
Let's get started!
Scenario: The Broken Quarterly Summary

Imagine you're the office manager at Velmix, a drinks company that supplies juices and sparkling waters to supermarket chains. The quarterly sales summary is due this week — and when you open it, one column is a wall of "#REF!" errors.
The old flow here is demanding: patch cells by hand, or hunt a forum for a formula that looks similar, and hope for the best.
With Claude in the sidebar, the playbook changes. But the first move isn't simply "fix it." It's finding out what the formula was supposed to do.
Explain First
Click the broken cell. The formula bar shows what the colleague left behind.
Your first move is to translate it. Ask Claude to explain the formula in plain language before anything gets touched.

blocks.exampleResponse: In plain terms: D5 takes the product code in A5 and looks it up in a table that used to sit in columns G–J, pulling the 3rd column — the quarterly volume. The #REF! means those columns were deleted, so the formula points at nothing. The logic is intact; only the reference is gone.
blocks.prompt: Ask Claude to explain the broken formula in plain language before fixing anything.
blocks.template: [Command] what the formula in D5 does in plain language, tell me what it needs to work, and [constraint] anything yet.

blocks.text: Now you know three things you didn't a minute ago: what the formula does, why it's broken, and what "fixed" should look like.
That last one matters most: you can't judge a repair if you don't know the intent.
A formula you can restate in plain language is a formula you can safely change. Translation first, repair second — especially with formulas you didn't write.
blocks.title: 💡 Explain Before You Edit

blocks.text: Find the Cause, Not the Symptom
The error code tells you where it hurts. It doesn't tell you why.
The why lives one level deeper — a deleted side table pulled the ground out from under this formula. Ask Claude to trace it and propose a repair, still hands-off.

blocks.exampleResponse: Root cause: the lookup table lived in columns G–J on this tab. When those columns were deleted last week, every VLOOKUP pointing there broke — that's all 38 errors in column D, one cause. The "Products" tab still holds the same data, so the fix is to point the lookups there instead of rebuilding the columns. Want me to apply it? I'll highlight every cell I touch.
blocks.prompt: Have Claude find why the column broke and propose a repair — without changing anything yet.
blocks.template: Trace why column D shows [error code], find the root cause, and propose a fix — [command] before changing anything.

blocks.text: One deletion, 38 broken cells, one fix — that's what tracing the cause buys you. Patching cell by cell would have treated 38 symptoms.
You approve the plan, and Claude rewrites the lookups to point at the "Products" tab — highlighting every cell it changes, with a note on what changed and why.
Review Like a Pro
Highlighted cells are an invitation. Scan them before you move on: do the changed cells match the plan you approved?
And if anything looks wrong, nothing is lost — Excel's regular undo works on Claude's changes too.

feedbackCorrect.text: You got it! Errors disappearing means the formula runs, not that it's right. The proof lives downstream: totals recompute, and a number you can verify independently comes out true.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A clean-looking column only proves the formula runs — a wrong reference can produce tidy, wrong numbers. Check what the formula feeds: the totals downstream, plus one value you know from elsewhere.

options.label: Claude confirmed the fix was applied successfully
The file saves without any warnings
No error codes are visible anywhere in the column
The quarterly totals recompute — and a spot-check against a value you know holds up

blocks.question: The fix is in, and the errors are gone. What actually tells you the repair worked?

blocks.text: Errors have locations and causes — repair the cause, then verify one level below it. A fix is real when the totals it feeds come out right, not when the error stops showing.
blocks.title: 💡 Fix the Cause, Check Downstream

blocks.text: Now Build One From Scratch
The summary works again — and immediately shows a gap. Velmix launched new drinks this quarter, and their product codes sit in the sales data with no names next to them.
Column B needs a formula that doesn't exist yet. You won't write it. You'll describe it — including what should happen when a code has no match.
Two constraints make the formula easy to maintain:

• Ask for the simplest version that does the job; no need for overcomplication.
  • Explain what happens when data is missing, so a missing code never breaks the sheet.

blocks.exampleResponse: Done — B5 now holds: =IFERROR(VLOOKUP($A5,Products!$A:$B,2,FALSE),"Not listed"). In one line: take the code in A5, find its name on the "Products" tab, and say "Not listed" instead of erroring when the code isn't there. Filled down through B42, all changes highlighted. Two cells currently show "Not listed" — the new launches, as expected.
blocks.prompt: Build the missing formula by describing its goal, its simplicity, and its missing-data behavior.
blocks.template: Write the [output] for column B that pulls each product's name from the "Products" tab, shows [label] when the code has no match, and [command] in one line.

blocks.text: Built Isn't Finished
Good job! The formula runs, the names appear, and two "Not listed" cells sit exactly where the new launches should be. Tempting to call it done.
But a formula earns trust the same way a repair does — by surviving the case built to break it. That's an evaluation, and it's a request like any other.

blocks.exampleResponse: Tested with a fake code, XX-999: shows "Not listed", no error, and the row 45 totals still calculate — text entries are skipped by the sums, so nothing breaks. One flag: a blank cell in column A also shows "Not listed." If blanks should stay blank instead, say the word and I'll add that rule.
blocks.prompt: Evaluate the new formula — feed it the breaking case and check what it feeds downstream.
blocks.template: [Command] the new formula on an edge case — a code that isn't in the "Products" tab — check the totals in row 45 still calculate, and flag anything the formula [condition].

blocks.text: Notice that the test surfaced a decision. Blanks and missing codes were about to be treated the same, and nobody had chosen that.
Evaluating turns silent assumptions into questions you get to answer.

A formula is finished when it survives the case designed to break it.

The loop is: Explain, fix, build. Evaluation is the habit that closes all three.
blocks.title: 💡 Build, Then Test

blocks.text: The Full Formula Rhythm
Look at what just happened to the workbook problem:

• You've translated a broken formula into plain language.
  • You've traced its root cause and repaired it in one pass.
  • You've built a missing formula from a single description.
And you proved everything with a reliable test. Good job!

• Explain before you edit: A formula you can restate in plain language is one you can safely change.
  • Trace causes, not symptoms: One deleted column can break 38 cells — repair the cause once.
  • Review the highlights: Claude marks every cell it touches; scan them before moving on, and remember undo works.
  • Describe to build: Ask for the simplest formula that does the job, and say what happens when data is missing.
  • Test before you trust: A formula is finished when it survives the case built to break it and its downstream totals hold.

Broken, missing, or brand-new — now formulas answer to you.
Next, you'll focus on cleaning data: an export where nothing is broken, but untidy — with duplicates, mixed formats, blanks. You'll turn that into a dataset worth analyzing.
Let's keep going!

Last lesson, formulas answered to you. This lesson takes on a different angle: the export where nothing is broken, but everything is untidy.
You'll turn a raw system export full of duplicates, mixed formats, and blanks into a dataset worth analyzing. By the end of the lesson, next month's export will arrive cleaner on its own.
Let's get started!
Scenario: The Monthly Export
Imagine you're the sales operations specialist at Vendaflow, a subscription service that delivers snack boxes to office kitchens. Every month, the order system produces a customer export.
Today it arrived messy:

• The same companies are spelled 3 ways.
  • Dates appeared in 2 formats.
  • Amounts are with and without currency signs.
  • Blanks are scattered through the revenue column.
Your analysis is due this evening. Cleaning the data by hand alone will take a full day. But there's a smarter approach. Let's try it out!
First move, same as any unfamiliar file: look before you touch. Ask for a damage report — with strict instructions to change nothing.

blocks.exampleResponse: Scanned 512 rows. Findings: 74 rows carry inconsistent company spellings — case, spacing, endings like "Ltd"; 212 dates use a second format (03/14/2026 instead of 2026-03-14); 46 amounts are stored as text with currency signs; 19 amounts are blank; and 23 groups of rows look like duplicates. Nothing changed — want the cleaning plan?

blocks.text: Nicely done! One reply, and the mess has a shape: 5 problems, each with a count.
A Useful Chip
The sidebar has a chip for exactly this — "/clean-data-xls": one command that standardizes, merges, and tidies in a single run.
This routine runs in a fixed order:

• Survey the sheet.
  • Ask you about the decisions it can't make on its own.
  • Lay out a plan
  • Ask permission before each change
  • Report what it did.
Click "/clean-data-xls", and the command lands in the reply box with a short description attached.
Whatever you type after it guides how the run works. And that's where your custom rules go. Let's practice!

Nice work! Claude surveys the sheet and stops with a question:
"19 rows have blank amounts. How should I handle them?", followed by tappable options.
No matter how carefully you plan a routine, it will eventually face a decision you didn’t anticipate. Let's see how a well-built routine handles it.

feedbackCorrect.text: That's right! A blank means nobody knows the number yet. Filling it from a pattern doesn't find the number — it invents one, and by next week it looks exactly like a real amount. Flagged blanks stay visible until someone chases the true figure.

feedbackIncorrect.text: These 19 amounts feed your revenue totals, so a guess in that column becomes a guess in every report built on it. A pattern-fill hides the gap, deleting rows hides the customer, and skipping hands the call to a routine that just told you it can't make it. Decision made, Claude lays out its plan — numbered steps, in order:

• Standardize the spellings
  • Convert the dates
  • Turn text amounts into numbers
  • Merge duplicates by your rule
  • Flag the blanks
  • Organize the block into a structured table.
As Claude executes your plan, it will stop and ask you two types of questions:

• Judgment — how should I treat this data? You're guarding the meaning.
  • Permission — may I change this? You're guarding the file.
Asking For Permissions
The first one arrives right away: "Claude wants to fix formulas in row 5."
Three ways to answer:

• Allow once — one change, then ask me again.
  • Always allow — stop asking for this kind of edit in this run.
  • Deny — don't do it.

Answers Your Manager Will Trust

A spreadsheet can give you a number in seconds, but understanding whether that number is worth acting on takes more than reading the result. That becomes especially important when someone asks you to explain what’s behind it.

In this lesson, you'll dig past the surface of your data to where the real answer lives, catch a figure that's confidently wrong, and test what happens when you change an assumption — all without breaking a single formula.
Let's get started!
Scenario: The Margin Dip
Imagine you're a category manager at Velmix — the drinks company whose quarterly summary you repaired earlier in this course. That file has grown up: it now carries prices, costs, and a margin model.
This morning, your manager sends one line: "Margin is down. I need to know why by Thursday."
You could paste that question straight into the sidebar. But there's one word in it worth slowing down for: margin.

It can mean gross margin, margin after discounts, margin after shipping — and each one gives a different answer. Claude will use whichever definition it finds. So you name the one you mean, and ask it to elaborate on the assumption.

blocks.exampleResponse: Using margin = revenue after retailer discounts, minus cost of goods. Q1: 28.8%. Q2: 25.8% — down 3.0 points. Q2 revenue is $787,378 with $203,153 of margin. Assumption stated: I used the discount rates on the Assumptions tab, not the ones written into individual orders. Cited: Summary E4:E6.
blocks.prompt: Ask the headline question — and pin down what "margin" means before Claude picks for you.
blocks.template: Compare Q1 and Q2 margin, where margin means [definition]. Show the change in points, and [transparency rule] you made.

blocks.text: The dip is confirmed: 3.0 points, measured the way you defined it.
But that 28.8% is a company-wide average — every region, every product, blended into 1 number. It tells you the margin fell, but not yet where or why.
Go Where the Answer Lives
The why lives one level down — in the regions, the categories, the months. So you break the number apart and look for the piece that moved.

blocks.exampleResponse: Margin % by region, Q1 → Q2: North 29.6% → 20.9%, down 8.7 points. South 28.1% → 28.0%. East 29.0% → 28.8%. West 27.8% → 27.6%. The other 3 regions are flat — the entire company dip comes from North. Cited: Summary B9:D12.
blocks.prompt: Split the margin dip by region and find where it concentrates.
blocks.template: Break the margin change down [dimension], compare Q1 and Q2 for each, and [command] the biggest drop.

blocks.text: Good job! 3 regions barely moved. North fell by 8.7 points, dragging the company down with it.
One follow-up: "Why did North's margin fall?" and Claude traces it to a single cell on the Assumptions tab: North's retailer discount went from 8% in Q1 to 18% in Q2. A chain renegotiated.
A company-wide number is where the question starts. Break it by region, category, or month, and the cause usually shows up in 1 piece.

blocks.text: Now Ask "What If?"
You know the cause: North's discount doubled. The obvious next question is the one your manager will ask on Thursday — how much would we get back if we pulled it down?
On the Assumptions tab, the blue cells are inputs. Change one, and every formula that depends on it recalculates: 1,400 order rows, every rollup, the headline.
Without a live model, testing an idea means copying the whole sheet to a new tab, retyping numbers, and hoping you didn't miss a cell.
Here, you change the input and read the result. The formulas stay exactly as they are.

blocks.exampleResponse: Changed Assumptions C6 from 18.0% to 12.0% — one cell, no formulas touched. Q2 margin % rises from 25.8% to 27.6%, and margin in dollars from $203,153 to $222,333: a gain of $19,180. North alone recovers from 20.9% to 26.3%. Every changed cell is highlighted.
blocks.prompt: Test the recovery — change the input, keep every formula untouched.
blocks.template: On the Assumptions tab, set North's Q2 discount to [new value]. [Constraint] any formulas. Show me the new Q2 margin and [comparison].

blocks.text: Nicely done! $19,180 back from editing one cell.
But a discount you can pull back is one you have to negotiate. So before recommending it, put it next to the alternative.
Two Scenarios, Side by Side
A number means more when it's standing next to another one.
The second option: leave the discount alone and raise list prices 3% across the board. Same model, but this time you’ll change a different input: the price uplift.

blocks.exampleResponse: Scenario A — North discount to 12%: margin 27.6%, $222,333 (+$19,180). Scenario B — 3% price uplift: margin 28.0%, $226,774 (+$23,621). B earns more, but it raises prices in 3 regions that never had a problem, and it assumes no customer buys less at the higher price. A targets the region where the margin actually went.
blocks.prompt: Run both scenarios and lay them side by side with the trade-off named.
blocks.template: [Command] 2 scenarios: North's discount back to 12%, and a 3% price uplift for everyone. Show Q2 margin for each, [output], and name [decision factor].

blocks.text: Now you have a clear comparison:

• Scenario B looks better by $4,441, and that's exactly why you asked for the trade-off.
  • Extra margin in scenario B assumes nobody buys less at a higher price, and it raises prices in 3 regions that did nothing wrong.
  • Scenario A costs less, and it fixes the thing that actually broke.
A single scenario shows one possible outcome. Comparing two scenarios using the same criteria makes the trade-offs clear and supports a stronger recommendation.
blocks.title: 💡 Compare Before You Recommend

blocks.text: Thursday, Solved
Nice work! You've prepared your analysis and are now ready for the report:

• Margin fell 3.0 points. It's all North, where the discount went from 8% to 18%.
  • Two products are unpriced, dragging down every category figure.
  • Pulling North back to 12% returns $19,180. A price rise would earn more and cost more trust.
A strong analysis usually moves through the same five questions:

• What changed? Establish the result or movement you need to explain.
  • Where did it change? Break the headline number down to find where the movement is concentrated.
  • Why did it change? Trace the result back to the inputs, assumptions, or events behind it.
  • Can I trust it? Check what was included, excluded, missing, or assumed.
  • What should we do? Test possible actions and compare their trade-offs.
The data and business question will change, but this sequence gives you a reliable way to investigate both.

• Define the measure before you analyze it: Make key terms explicit so Claude works from the same definition you do.
  • Move from the headline to the driver: Break results down by the dimensions that matter, then trace the biggest movement back to its source.
  • Verify before you interpret: Check totals, blanks, zeros, missing records, and assumptions before turning a result into a conclusion.
  • Use what-if analysis to isolate effects: Change one assumption at a time when you need to understand how that input affects the model.
  • Compare options on the same criteria: Look at the outcome, the assumptions behind it, and the trade-offs before making a recommendation.

A spreadsheet can give you a number in seconds, but understanding whether that number is worth acting on takes more than reading the result. That becomes especially important when someone asks you to explain what’s behind it.

In this lesson, you'll dig past the surface of your data to where the real answer lives, catch a figure that's confidently wrong, and test what happens when you change an assumption — all without breaking a single formula.
Let's get started!
Scenario: The Margin Dip
Imagine you're a category manager at Velmix — the drinks company whose quarterly summary you repaired earlier in this course. That file has grown up: it now carries prices, costs, and a margin model.
This morning, your manager sends one line: "Margin is down. I need to know why by Thursday."
You could paste that question straight into the sidebar. But there's one word in it worth slowing down for: margin.

It can mean gross margin, margin after discounts, margin after shipping — and each one gives a different answer. Claude will use whichever definition it finds. So you name the one you mean, and ask it to elaborate on the assumption.

blocks.text: The dip is confirmed: 3.0 points, measured the way you defined it.
But that 28.8% is a company-wide average — every region, every product, blended into 1 number. It tells you the margin fell, but not yet where or why.
Go Where the Answer Lives
The why lives one level down — in the regions, the categories, the months. So you break the number apart and look for the piece that moved.

blocks.exampleResponse: Margin % by region, Q1 → Q2: North 29.6% → 20.9%, down 8.7 points. South 28.1% → 28.0%. East 29.0% → 28.8%. West 27.8% → 27.6%. The other 3 regions are flat — the entire company dip comes from North. Cited: Summary B9:D12.

blocks.template: Break the margin change down [dimension], compare Q1 and Q2 for each, and [command] the biggest drop.

blocks.text: Good job! 3 regions barely moved. North fell by 8.7 points, dragging the company down with it.
One follow-up: "Why did North's margin fall?" and Claude traces it to a single cell on the Assumptions tab: North's retailer discount went from 8% in Q1 to 18% in Q2. A chain renegotiated.

You know the cause: North's discount doubled. The obvious next question is the one your manager will ask on Thursday — how much would we get back if we pulled it down?
On the Assumptions tab, the blue cells are inputs. Change one, and every formula that depends on it recalculates: 1,400 order rows, every rollup, the headline.

A Clear View of 2K Rows
A transaction log can contain everything you need — and still leave you hunting through hundreds of rows for one simple answer.
In this lesson, you'll turn a long order log into a PivotTable by describing the summary you need, reshaping it as new questions come up, and checking the result before you share it.
Let's get started!
Scenario: The Monthly Review
Imagine you're an account manager at Vendaflow, a snack-box supplier you met earlier in this course. The Orders tab has 1,872 rows — one order per row — and your monthly review is tomorrow.
Your manager needs to see sales by product, region, and quarter. The detail is all there, and now you need the summary.
You could build a grid of formulas for every product and quarter. But this question has a different shape: the same measure needs to be grouped and compared across several categories.
That's where a PivotTable is a better fit.
A PivotTable turns a long list of rows into a compact summary. You choose what to group, what to compare, and which number to calculate without building a separate formula for every combination.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! The question asks for the same measure — revenue — grouped by product and quarter. A PivotTable can summarize the full order log in one view.

blocks.question: "How much revenue did each product generate in each quarter?"

blocks.text: Start With the Question
Before you build the PivotTable, name the question it needs to answer:
"How much revenue did each product generate in each quarter?"
That question already contains the layout.

• The product gives you the rows because you want to compare one product with another.
  • Quarter gives you the columns because you want to see how those products change across time.
  • Revenue gives you the values because that’s the number you want to calculate and compare.
And because the question asks for the revenue, the values need to be added together using "Sum".
Rows hold the groups you want to compare. Columns split them across another dimension. Values hold the measure and the calculation, such as Sum, Average, or Count.
blocks.title: 💡 A Pivot Is a Question With a Layout

blocks.prompt: Turn the question into a PivotTable layout.
blocks.template: [Command] a PivotTable from the Orders data. Put [row field] in rows, [column field] in columns, and Revenue in values summarized by [aggregation]. Place it on a new sheet named Quarterly Sales.

blocks.text: Nicely done! 1,872 orders are now a compact summary of four products across four quarters.
Claude may ask for permission before changing the workbook. Review the proposed change, then allow it when the requested layout matches what you asked for.
The first useful view is ready — but it won't be the last question your manager asks.
The First Layout Is a Starting Point
Your manager looks at Q4 and asks: "Is the growth spread across the business, or is one region driving it?"
The current view has Product and Quarter, but no Region. You don't need to rearrange the PivotTable manually. Ask Claude to reshape it around the next question.

blocks.prompt: Extend the summary with the dimension the next question needs.
blocks.template: Keep Product in rows and Quarter in columns. Add [dimension] to [placement] so I can view the same summary one region at a time. Keep Revenue summarized by Sum.

blocks.text: Good job! The same PivotTable can now answer the product-by-quarter question for the whole business or for one region at a time.
The source data hasn't changed. You changed how the summary is viewed.
Change What the Summary Measures
Total revenue tells you how much came in. But it doesn't tell you whether Q4 growth was driven by more orders or by larger orders.
The same data can answer that question too — you just need different calculations in Values.
Because each row represents one order and every order has an Order ID, Count of Order ID gives you the number of orders.
The Average of Revenue gives you the average revenue per order.
You can place both next to total revenue and compare all three.

blocks.prompt: Add the measures that explain how the total changed.
blocks.template: Add [field] to Values summarized by [aggregation] to show order volume. Add Revenue to Values again and summarize it by Average. Keep Sum of Revenue. Then compare Q3 and Q4 across all three measures.

blocks.text: Nicely done! Q4 had 41 more orders than Q3, while average revenue per order increased by only about $2.
The total went up mainly because Vendaflow received more orders, not because individual orders became much larger.

• Sum answers how much.
  • Count answers how many.
  • Average answers how large each record is on average.

Choose the calculation that matches the question you're trying to answer.
blocks.title: 💡 The Calculation Changes the Question

blocks.text: One Answer Raises the Next Question
Now you know that more orders drove most of the Q4 growth. The next question is: "Where did that growth come from?"
The Region is already part of the PivotTable. Ask Claude to restructure the summary so the regions can be compared directly.

blocks.prompt: Reshape the summary around the next question.
blocks.template: Restructure the PivotTable so [dimension] appears above Product in Rows. Keep Quarter in Columns and only Sum of Revenue in Values.

blocks.text: Good job! You didn't have to return to the order log and build another summary by hand. You changed the question, and Claude reshaped the PivotTable around it.
That flexibility is useful, but before the numbers go into the monthly review, the summary needs one final check.
Before It Leaves the Workbook
A PivotTable is a summary of the source data. Before you present it, make sure its Grand Total reconciles with the data it came from.
For this view, total revenue in the PivotTable should equal total revenue in Orders.

blocks.exampleResponse:
They match exactly — no difference.
  • PivotTable Grand Total (Quarterly SalesF25): $1,208,600
  • Sum of Revenue in Orders (OrdersI2:I1873): $1,208,600 across all 1,872 order rows
Every revenue cell in the source is numeric (no blanks or text values that would be silently excluded), so the pivot is aggregating the complete dataset. The totals tie out. I didn't change anything.
blocks.prompt: Check the summary against its source before sharing it.
blocks.template: [Command] the PivotTable Grand Total with the total Revenue in Orders. [Constraint]. Tell me whether they match, and explain any difference.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! The numbers may be correct for West, but they don't represent the whole company. Clear the filter or label the view correctly before sharing it.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The PivotTable may be calculating the filtered data correctly, but the title claims a wider scope. Check the active filters before presenting the result.

blocks.instruction: Check whether the summary matches the claim you're making.
blocks.question: You return to the product view. Its title says "Company Sales," but Region is filtered to West.

blocks.text: A total can be correct for a filtered view and still be wrong for the claim you're making. Reconcile the numbers, then check which filters and groups are shaping the view.
blocks.title: 💡 Check the Scope as Well as the Total

blocks.text: Review, Ready
Nice work! The 1,872-row order log now gives you the views the monthly review needed:

• Product sales across quarters.
  • The same summary filtered by region.
  • Order count and average order value when the total needed explanation.
  • Regional and product breakdowns when the next question came up.
  • A Grand Total checked against the source data
The process stays the same:

• Name the question.
  • Choose the groups: what belongs in rows, columns, or filters?
  • Choose the measure: what belongs in values, and how should it be calculated?
  • Reshape the view when the next question appears.
  • Reconcile the result before you share it.

A transaction log can contain everything you need — and still leave you hunting through hundreds of rows for one simple answer.
In this lesson, you'll turn a long order log into a PivotTable by describing the summary you need, reshaping it as new questions come up, and checking the result before you share it.
Let's get started!
Scenario: The Monthly Review
Imagine you're an account manager at Vendaflow, a snack-box supplier you met earlier in this course. The Orders tab has 1,872 rows — one order per row — and your monthly review is tomorrow.
Your manager needs to see sales by product, region, and quarter. The detail is all there, and now you need the summary.
You could build a grid of formulas for every product and quarter. But this question has a different shape: the same measure needs to be grouped and compared across several categories.
That's where a PivotTable is a better fit.
A PivotTable turns a long list of rows into a compact summary. You choose what to group, what to compare, and which number to calculate without building a separate formula for every combination.
blocks.title: 💡 What Is a PivotTable?

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! The question asks for the same measure — revenue — grouped by product and quarter. A PivotTable can summarize the full order log in one view.

feedbackIncorrect.text: You could calculate the answer with formulas, but a PivotTable is a better fit when the same measure needs to be grouped across several categories.

blocks.instruction: Choose the better tool for the question.
blocks.question: "How much revenue did each product generate in each quarter?"

blocks.text: Start With the Question
Before you build the PivotTable, name the question it needs to answer:
"How much revenue did each product generate in each quarter?"
That question already contains the layout.

• The product gives you the rows because you want to compare one product with another.
  • Quarter gives you the columns because you want to see how those products change across time.
  • Revenue gives you the values because that’s the number you want to calculate and compare.
And because the question asks for the revenue, the values need to be added together using "Sum".
Rows hold the groups you want to compare. Columns split them across another dimension. Values hold the measure and the calculation, such as Sum, Average, or Count.
blocks.title: 💡 A Pivot Is a Question With a Layout

screens.title: 💡 A Pivot Is a Question With a Layout

blocks.prompt: Turn the question into a PivotTable layout.
blocks.template: [Command] a PivotTable from the Orders data. Put [row field] in rows, [column field] in columns, and Revenue in values summarized by [aggregation]. Place it on a new sheet named Quarterly Sales.

blocks.text: Nicely done! 1,872 orders are now a compact summary of four products across four quarters.
Claude may ask for permission before changing the workbook. Review the proposed change, then allow it when the requested layout matches what you asked for.
The first useful view is ready — but it won't be the last question your manager asks.
The First Layout Is a Starting Point
Your manager looks at Q4 and asks: "Is the growth spread across the business, or is one region driving it?"
The current view has Product and Quarter, but no Region. You don't need to rearrange the PivotTable manually. Ask Claude to reshape it around the next question.

blocks.prompt: Extend the summary with the dimension the next question needs.
blocks.template: Keep Product in rows and Quarter in columns. Add [dimension] to [placement] so I can view the same summary one region at a time. Keep Revenue summarized by Sum.

blocks.text: Good job! The same PivotTable can now answer the product-by-quarter question for the whole business or for one region at a time.
The source data hasn't changed. You changed how the summary is viewed.
Change What the Summary Measures
Total revenue tells you how much came in. But it doesn't tell you whether Q4 growth was driven by more orders or by larger orders.
The same data can answer that question too — you just need different calculations in Values.
Because each row represents one order and every order has an Order ID, Count of Order ID gives you the number of orders.
The Average of Revenue gives you the average revenue per order.
You can place both next to total revenue and compare all three.

blocks.prompt: Add the measures that explain how the total changed.
blocks.template: Add [field] to Values summarized by [aggregation] to show order volume. Add Revenue to Values again and summarize it by Average. Keep Sum of Revenue. Then compare Q3 and Q4 across all three measures.

blocks.text: Nicely done! Q4 had 41 more orders than Q3, while average revenue per order increased by only about $2.
The total went up mainly because Vendaflow received more orders, not because individual orders became much larger.

• Sum answers how much.
  • Count answers how many.
  • Average answers how large each record is on average.

Choose the calculation that matches the question you're trying to answer.
blocks.title: 💡 The Calculation Changes the Question

blocks.text: One Answer Raises the Next Question
Now you know that more orders drove most of the Q4 growth. The next question is: "Where did that growth come from?"
The Region is already part of the PivotTable. Ask Claude to restructure the summary so the regions can be compared directly.

blocks.prompt: Reshape the summary around the next question.
blocks.template: Restructure the PivotTable so [dimension] appears above Product in Rows. Keep Quarter in Columns and only Sum of Revenue in Values.

blocks.text: Good job! You didn't have to return to the order log and build another summary by hand. You changed the question, and Claude reshaped the PivotTable around it.
That flexibility is useful, but before the numbers go into the monthly review, the summary needs one final check.
Before It Leaves the Workbook
A PivotTable is a summary of the source data. Before you present it, make sure its Grand Total reconciles with the data it came from.
For this view, total revenue in the PivotTable should equal total revenue in Orders.

blocks.exampleResponse:
They match exactly — no difference.
  • PivotTable Grand Total (Quarterly SalesF25): $1,208,600
  • Sum of Revenue in Orders (OrdersI2:I1873): $1,208,600 across all 1,872 order rows
Every revenue cell in the source is numeric (no blanks or text values that would be silently excluded), so the pivot is aggregating the complete dataset. The totals tie out. I didn't change anything.
blocks.prompt: Check the summary against its source before sharing it.
blocks.template: [Command] the PivotTable Grand Total with the total Revenue in Orders. [Constraint]. Tell me whether they match, and explain any difference.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! The numbers may be correct for West, but they don't represent the whole company. Clear the filter or label the view correctly before sharing it.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The PivotTable may be calculating the filtered data correctly, but the title claims a wider scope. Check the active filters before presenting the result.

blocks.instruction: Check whether the summary matches the claim you're making.
blocks.question: You return to the product view. Its title says "Company Sales," but Region is filtered to West.

blocks.text: A total can be correct for a filtered view and still be wrong for the claim you're making. Reconcile the numbers, then check which filters and groups are shaping the view.
blocks.title: 💡 Check the Scope as Well as the Total

screens.title: 💡 Check the Scope as Well as the Total

blocks.text: Review, Ready
Nice work! The 1,872-row order log now gives you the views the monthly review needed:

• Product sales across quarters.
  • The same summary filtered by region.
  • Order count and average order value when the total needed explanation.
  • Regional and product breakdowns when the next question came up.
  • A Grand Total checked against the source data
The process stays the same:

• Name the question.
  • Choose the groups: what belongs in rows, columns, or filters?
  • Choose the measure: what belongs in values, and how should it be calculated?
  • Reshape the view when the next question appears.
  • Reconcile the result before you share it.

• Use a PivotTable for grouped summaries: It's a strong fit when the same measure needs to be compared across categories, periods, or other dimensions.
  • Describe the layout clearly: Name what belongs in rows, columns, filters, and values — and how the values should be calculated.
  • Treat the first layout as a starting point: When the question changes, ask Claude for the layout the next question needs.
  • Match the calculation to the question: Sum, Count, and Total.
  • Verify before you present: Reconcile the Grand Total with the source and check the scope of any active filters.

blocks.text: What's Next?
Great job! You've turned a long transaction log into summaries that can change as the questions change without rebuilding every view by hand.

Next, you'll turn those verified summaries into charts and a one-screen dashboard. You'll choose each visual based on the message it needs to show, then trace every displayed number back to the summary behind it.

The Story in One Screen
A workbook can contain the right numbers, but for a presentation, it might not be enough. The data visualization is what Claude for Excel can help you with!
In this lesson, you'll turn verified summaries into charts people can read quickly, build a one-screen dashboard, and check every displayed number before you present it.
Let's get started!
Scenario: Twelve Tabs, No Story
Imagine you're a team lead at Northframe. The monthly review runs on a workbook with twelve tabs: revenue, margins, regions, monthly trends, and the summary tables behind them.
The numbers are ready. Your job is to turn the quarter into one screen that answers two questions: What changed? And where did it come from?
The first decision is the message the visual needs to convey, making it easy to see.
Different questions have different shapes:

• Trend: How did something change over time? Better convey in a line chart.
  • Comparison: Which category is higher or lower? Better convey in a bar chart.
  • Composition: How is a whole divided into parts? Better convey in a donut chart.
Choose the message first. Then choose the chart.

blocks.text: Start with the question the visual needs to answer. Once you know whether you're showing a trend, comparison, or composition, the chart choice becomes much easier.
blocks.title: 💡 Name the Message Before the Chart

blocks.text: Start With the Trend
Your first question is:
"How has revenue moved across the year, and what happened in the latest quarter?"
The Monthly Summary tab has one revenue figure for each month from January to December. The order matters because time is a sequence.
That makes a line chart a natural starting point.

blocks.prompt: Turn the monthly summary into a chart that shows movement over time.
blocks.template: [Command] a [chart] from the Monthly Summary showing Month on the horizontal axis and Revenue on the vertical axis. Title it "Monthly Revenue Trend" and place it on a new sheet named [sheet name].

blocks.text: Nicely done! The chart now shows the full year in one view. Revenue softened in September, then rose through each month of Q4.
The data is correct, but a correct chart isn't automatically effective. Your audience still needs to see the main point quickly.
Describe the Read You Want
You could tell Claude which individual chart elements to change one by one.
Or you can describe the result you need:
"Make the Q4 acceleration easy to see at a glance for a leadership audience."
That gives Claude a clearer goal for the whole visual.

blocks.prompt: Refine the chart around what the audience should notice.
blocks.template: Restyle the Monthly Revenue Trend so [message] is easy to see at a glance for [audience]. Reduce visual clutter, keep the labels readable, and don't change the underlying data.

blocks.text: Good job! The chart still shows the same twelve numbers. What changed is the reading experience: the latest movement is easier to find, and details that don't help the message get less attention.
Tell Claude what the audience should notice and how quickly they should notice it. The goal of the chart matters more than a list of formatting instructions.
blocks.title: 💡 Describe the Read, Not Only the Feature

blocks.text: Find Where the Growth Came From
The trend shows that Q4 improved. The next question is where that increase came from.
The Regional Summary compares Q3 and Q4 revenue across North, South, East, and West.
You could use another line chart. But regions aren't points in a sequence.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! The regions are separate categories, not a sequence. A bar chart makes the differences between them easier to compare.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Connecting North, South, East, and West with a line suggests a sequence that isn't really there. A bar chart fits a category comparison better.

blocks.instruction: Decide whether the chart shape fits the question.
blocks.question: You need to compare Q3 and Q4 revenue across four regions. Should you use a line chart?

blocks.prompt: Compare the regions and make the biggest change easy to find.
blocks.template: Create a [chart type] from the Regional Summary comparing Q3 and Q4 [comparison data] by Region. Place it below the monthly trend on Dashboard and make the region with the largest increase easy to identify at a glance.

blocks.text: Nicely done! The breakdown shows that Q4 revenue increased across the regions, but not equally.
North had the largest increase, contributing $80,000 of the $195,000 gain from Q3 to Q4.
The trend told you what changed. The breakdown shows where the change came from.
From Two Charts to One Dashboard
You now have the two visuals the review needs:

• One trend showing how revenue moved across the year.
  • One breakdown showing how Q3 and Q4 compare by region.
Now they need context, as a viewer shouldn't have to calculate the headline result from the charts.
At the top of the dashboard, add three numbers that frame the quarter:
Q4 Revenue: $2.27M Growth vs. Q3: +9.4% Gross Margin: 34.1%
Then keep the monthly trend and regional breakdown underneath.
Three headline numbers, one trend, one breakdown. Everything on one screen.

blocks.prompt: Bring the headline figures and visuals together around one audience need.
blocks.template: Turn the Dashboard sheet into a one-screen summary for [audience]. At the top, show Q4 Revenue, Growth vs. Q3, and Gross Margin as three headline figures. Below them, keep the monthly revenue trend and the Q3 vs. Q4 [data]. [Command] so the quarter's main story can be understood quickly.

blocks.text: Good job! The twelve-tab workbook now has one place to start.
A viewer can see the quarter's scale, direction, and main regional driver without opening the source tabs first.
Finish Or Keep Going?
Imagine someone opens the dashboard just before the meeting.
Within 10 seconds, they should be able to answer:

• How did the quarter perform?
  • What changed over time?
  • Where did the change come from?
If the screen can't answer those questions quickly, adding more charts won't fix it.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! The dashboard already answers the main questions. Extra charts should earn their place by helping the audience make a decision, not by representing every table in the workbook.

feedbackIncorrect.text: More coverage doesn't automatically make the dashboard more useful. If the main questions are already answered, seven more charts make the story harder to find.

blocks.instruction: Judge the dashboard by the audience's question, not by how much information it contains.
blocks.question: The dashboard shows three headline figures, a monthly trend, and a regional breakdown. A colleague suggests adding seven more charts so every summary table is represented.

blocks.text: A dashboard doesn't need to display everything the workbook knows. It needs to make the most important answers easy to find for a specific audience.
blocks.title: 💡 A Dashboard Has a Job

blocks.text: Trace Every Number Back
The dashboard is clear. Now it needs to be trustworthy.
A large headline number or polished chart can still point to the wrong range, an outdated summary, or a filtered view.
Before the meeting, trace every dashboard element back to its verified summary.

blocks.exampleResponse: Got it. I’ll trace each headline figure and chart back to the summary or PivotTable that feeds it, confirm the displayed values match, and leave the dashboard unchanged while I audit it.
blocks.prompt: Check the presentation layer against the summaries that feed it.
blocks.template: Audit the Dashboard. For each headline figure and chart, [command] it back to the summary or PivotTable it uses and confirm the displayed figures match. [constraint].

blocks.text: Nicely done! Each displayed result now has a clear source.
The dashboard is the presentation layer. Its trust comes from the verified summaries underneath it.
Review, Ready
Nice work! The dashboard now gives leadership:

• Three headline figures for the quarter.
  • One trend showing how performance moved over time.
  • One breakdown showing where the change came from.
  • A layout that can be understood quickly.
  • A verified source behind every displayed result.

• Choose the chart from the message: Use the shape of the question to guide the visual.
  • Design for the intended read: Tell Claude what the audience should notice, not only which chart features to change.
  • Keep the dashboard focused: A few headline figures and purposeful visuals are more useful than a screen that reproduces every table.
  • Test the result against the audience's questions: A dashboard works when the important answers are easy to find quickly.
  • Verify the presentation layer: Trace every headline number and chart back to the summary or PivotTable behind it.

blocks.text: What's Next?
Great job! You've moved from raw data to verified summaries, and then turned those summaries into a dashboard people can quickly understand.
Next, you'll take the recurring work behind your reports and turn it into a repeatable workflow, so the process doesn't have to start from scratch every time.

blocks.text: Turn the Process Into a Skill

• When it should trigger
  • What it should produce

• The input

  • Output

blocks.text: Know What Each Layer Does

  • Use Cowork for recurring starts: A schedule can begin the work on a cadence, but the output still needs review before it is used or shared.

blocks.text: From Workbook to Workflow
Great job! You started this course by asking Claude questions about a workbook you didn't know.
Since then, you've learned to repair formulas, clean data, investigate results, build PivotTables, create dashboards, and turn a repeated reporting process into reusable work.
You can now move from a raw workbook to a recurring workflow, with Claude handling more of the execution as the process becomes clearer, and your judgment staying where it matters most.
